doc.title: Artie Shaw — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Studio musicians' attitudes; quitting at 23; Arnold Brilhart's praise
summary: Disciplined readers worked in the studios; Shaw quit at 23 for a Bucks County farm, then returned, and Brilhart recalls him as the natural player.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: When you got to New York, and a lot of those guys were in the studio scene as well . . .
The ones who could read, who were disciplined musicians, were in the studios, yeah.
. . . did they . . . What was the general attitude toward playing the music that they had to play every day? Were they frustrated by it? or . . .

I’ve written an awful lot about that. I was. I quit at 23. I quit the business. Went out and bought a so-called farm in Bucks County. Found I couldn’t write, and came back, and to support myself, had to go back into it.
But some of them didn’t mind it?
Mannie Klein didn’t mind it at all. I can’t think many of them did. Arnold Brillhardt calls me every now and then. He’s 84, 85 now. 86, I think.
I used to play his mouthpieces.

He was a good alto man. He said to me, “You were the guy. Everybody knew you were the natural guy. Benny [Goodman] had studied and played and worked like hell at it. You used to play things we couldn’t believe.” I said, “Really. You never told me. Where were you when?” He said, “We were rivals, looking for work.” But he’s very

kind. He’s been very, very . . . what’s the word? Flattering? I don’t think he’s flattering. I think he means it. I was the new kid on the block when I came in, you see. Benny was well established. Jimmy [Dorsey] had been there forever. And Tommy [Dorsey] was the big man in that business. And Mannie Klein and Charlie Margulis and Fuzzy Ferrar. I got to know all of them. Miff [Mole]. All these guys were legendary names to me.
